excerpts: Walk-forward optimization formalizes a habit a careful trader already has: re-fit periodically, and only ever judge yourself on the period after the fit.

You slice your history into consecutive windows. Each window has an **in-sample** segment, where you are allowed to run your full parameter search, and an **out-of-sample** segment immediately following it, where you take the single best in-sample parameter set and run it untouched. Then you slide the whole arrangement forward and repeat.

The result is a sequence of out-of-sample segments — none of which were ever used for optimization — laid end to end. Stitch their returns together and you have a _walk-forward equity curve_ . That curve is the honest one. It answers the question that actually matters: “If I had been re-optimizing this strategy on a schedule and trading it forward the whole time, what would have happened?”

**Rolling (sliding) window.** The in-sample period is a fixed length — say two years — that slides forward. You always optimize on the most recent two years, which means the strategy adapts to recent regimes and quietly forgets the distant past. Good if you believe markets are non-stationary (they are) and the relevant past is recent.

A rolling window keeps the in-sample period a fixed length that slides forward, so it always optimizes on the most recent data and adapts to changing regimes. An anchored window always starts at the beginning of your history and expands, using all available data and producing more stable but slower-adapting parameters. Rolling encodes a belief that recent past matters most; anchored encodes a belief in long-run stability.

**Anchored (expanding) window.** The in-sample period always starts at the beginning of your data and grows. Each re-optimization sees everything that ever happened. This is more stable, uses more data, and is more conservative, but it dilutes recent structure under a growing pile of old history.
An anchored window always starts at the beginning of your history and expands, using all available data and producing more stable but slower-adapting parameters.
Rolling encodes a belief that recent past matters most; anchored encodes a belief in long-run stability.
Neither is “correct” — they encode different beliefs about how much the past resembles the future.
I default to rolling windows for anything regime-sensitive (most price-action strategies) and anchored windows for slow factor work where I genuinely want the long-run average to dominate.

That is a search procedure with enough degrees of freedom to memorize the past. The technical name is overfitting, and in finance it has a particularly nasty form because the signal-to-noise ratio of returns is so low. When you grid-search a parameter space and keep the best result, you are running many quasi-independent trials and reporting the maximum. The expected maximum of a pile of noisy backtests is positive even when the true edge is zero — this is sometimes discussed under the banner of “the deflated Sharpe ratio” or “backtest overfitting,” and the core insight is brutal: the more parameter combinations you try, the higher your in-sample Sharpe will be _purely by luck_ . A single train/test split is the usual first defense, and it is better than nothing. You fit on 2015–2021, you test on 2022–2024, you report the test number. But it has two quiet problems. First, you only get one out-of-sample period, so your estimate of forward performance is one noisy draw — if 2022 happened to suit your strategy, you will never know.
You run the test, the result disappoints, you tweak the strategy, you run the test again. After a dozen iterations your “out-of-sample” period has leaked into your design decisions.

excerpts: Walk-forward optimization formalizes a habit a careful trader already has: re-fit periodically, and only ever judge yourself on the period after the fit.

You slice your history into consecutive windows. Each window has an **in-sample** segment, where you are allowed to run your full parameter search, and an **out-of-sample** segment immediately following it, where you take the single best in-sample parameter set and run it untouched. Then you slide the whole arrangement forward and repeat.

The result is a sequence of out-of-sample segments — none of which were ever used for optimization — laid end to end. Stitch their returns together and you have a _walk-forward equity curve_ . That curve is the honest one. It answers the question that actually matters: “If I had been re-optimizing this strategy on a schedule and trading it forward the whole time, what would have happened?”

**Rolling (sliding) window.** The in-sample period is a fixed length — say two years — that slides forward. You always optimize on the most recent two years, which means the strategy adapts to recent regimes and quietly forgets the distant past. Good if you believe markets are non-stationary (they are) and the relevant past is recent.

A rolling window keeps the in-sample period a fixed length that slides forward, so it always optimizes on the most recent data and adapts to changing regimes. An anchored window always starts at the beginning of your history and expands, using all available data and producing more stable but slower-adapting parameters. Rolling encodes a belief that recent past matters most; anchored encodes a belief in long-run stability.

**Anchored (expanding) window.** The in-sample period always starts at the beginning of your data and grows. Each re-optimization sees everything that ever happened. This is more stable, uses more data, and is more conservative, but it dilutes recent structure under a growing pile of old history.
An anchored window always starts at the beginning of your history and expands, using all available data and producing more stable but slower-adapting parameters.
Rolling encodes a belief that recent past matters most; anchored encodes a belief in long-run stability.
Neither is “correct” — they encode different beliefs about how much the past resembles the future.
I default to rolling windows for anything regime-sensitive (most price-action strategies) and anchored windows for slow factor work where I genuinely want the long-run average to dominate.

That is a search procedure with enough degrees of freedom to memorize the past. The technical name is overfitting, and in finance it has a particularly nasty form because the signal-to-noise ratio of returns is so low. When you grid-search a parameter space and keep the best result, you are running many quasi-independent trials and reporting the maximum. The expected maximum of a pile of noisy backtests is positive even when the true edge is zero — this is sometimes discussed under the banner of “the deflated Sharpe ratio” or “backtest overfitting,” and the core insight is brutal: the more parameter combinations you try, the higher your in-sample Sharpe will be _purely by luck_ . A single train/test split is the usual first defense, and it is better than nothing. You fit on 2015–2021, you test on 2022–2024, you report the test number. But it has two quiet problems. First, you only get one out-of-sample period, so your estimate of forward performance is one noisy draw — if 2022 happened to suit your strategy, you will never know.
You run the test, the result disappoints, you tweak the strategy, you run the test again. After a dozen iterations your “out-of-sample” period has leaked into your design decisions.

excerpts: Walk-forward optimization formalizes a habit a careful trader already has: re-fit periodically, and only ever judge yourself on the period after the fit.

You slice your history into consecutive windows. Each window has an **in-sample** segment, where you are allowed to run your full parameter search, and an **out-of-sample** segment immediately following it, where you take the single best in-sample parameter set and run it untouched. Then you slide the whole arrangement forward and repeat.

The result is a sequence of out-of-sample segments — none of which were ever used for optimization — laid end to end. Stitch their returns together and you have a _walk-forward equity curve_ . That curve is the honest one. It answers the question that actually matters: “If I had been re-optimizing this strategy on a schedule and trading it forward the whole time, what would have happened?”

**Rolling (sliding) window.** The in-sample period is a fixed length — say two years — that slides forward. You always optimize on the most recent two years, which means the strategy adapts to recent regimes and quietly forgets the distant past. Good if you believe markets are non-stationary (they are) and the relevant past is recent.

A rolling window keeps the in-sample period a fixed length that slides forward, so it always optimizes on the most recent data and adapts to changing regimes. An anchored window always starts at the beginning of your history and expands, using all available data and producing more stable but slower-adapting parameters. Rolling encodes a belief that recent past matters most; anchored encodes a belief in long-run stability.

**Anchored (expanding) window.** The in-sample period always starts at the beginning of your data and grows. Each re-optimization sees everything that ever happened. This is more stable, uses more data, and is more conservative, but it dilutes recent structure under a growing pile of old history.
An anchored window always starts at the beginning of your history and expands, using all available data and producing more stable but slower-adapting parameters.
Rolling encodes a belief that recent past matters most; anchored encodes a belief in long-run stability.
Neither is “correct” — they encode different beliefs about how much the past resembles the future.
I default to rolling windows for anything regime-sensitive (most price-action strategies) and anchored windows for slow factor work where I genuinely want the long-run average to dominate.

The label at \\(t\\) is therefore a function of prices up to \\(t + 5\\) . Now consider k-fold cross-validation. The training observation's label (not its features, but its label) was computed using prices through \\(t\_\\text{train} + 5\\) , which includes the test observation's window. The model trains on this label. The training label encodes information from the test period. Even with walk-forward's temporal ordering, if \\(t\_\\text{train}\\) precedes \\(t\_\\text{test}\\) by less than the label horizon, the training label reaches forward into the test fold. The result: the model performs better on the test fold than it would in live trading. The Sharpe is inflated. The bias is systematic — every training observation near the train-test boundary leaks. Naive k-fold on triple-barrier labels typically overstates Sharpe by 10-30% in standard setups. Purging ¶ The AFML correction: drop training observations whose label horizons overlap the test fold. For each observation \\(i\\) , define the label horizon \\(t\_1[i]\\) — the time at which its label is realized. Even when no label horizon crosses the test-fold boundary, consecutive observations in a time series tend to be correlated — prices, volumes, implied volatilities all show some degree of autocorrelation. Classification accuracy can be a diagnostic, but it is not a substitute for the return or risk-adjusted performance that the trading decision actually optimizes. The ranking procedure is generic across performance metrics, including Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Jensen's Alpha, and Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio. [executive_summary[4]] [8]
- **Window Regime**: Expanding windows use all history from a fixed start and grow; rolling windows use a fixed-length recent-history window [executive_summary[0]] [6]. The former favors sample size and stability, while the latter favors adaptation and forgets older regimes. Treat the choice and window length as model assumptions, not as free post hoc knobs.
- **Engineering Isolation**: Every fold needs its own fitted preprocessing, model state, feature-selection state, and artifacts. A fold must never read a model written by another fold or write to a production path that a later fold can load. I added a small public validation sample that keeps the protocol explicit: walk-forward folds, train-only preprocessing, validation-only selection, untouched test evaluation, and a [executive_summary[5]] [10]
- **Granularity Discipline**: Evaluate every OOS event or bar required by the declared execution policy. Striding through OOS bars to save time changes the return distribution, can omit trades, and makes the resulting equity curve a different experiment.

The practical answer is not to choose one label among WFO, CPCV, and PBO. They solve different problems. WFO is a chronological simulation of deployment. CPCV is a way to create many purged train/test combinations and reconstruct multiple possible OOS paths. PBO is a selection-bias statistic computed from a CSCV performance-ranking experiment. A robust research program can use all three, followed by one genuinely untouched final holdout.
content.walk_forward_folds_simulate_the_actual_r:
Time-series splitting exists because ordinary random cross-validation can train on future observations and evaluate on past observations; the scikit-learn time-series documentation states this temporal constraint directly [walk_forward_folds_simulate_the_actual_retraining_rule[0]] [9]. Walk-forward validation makes the constraint operational: choose an in-sample interval, fit the complete candidate pipeline, run it on the next OOS interval without changing the fitted state, and concatenate the OOS intervals in time order [walk_forward_folds_simulate_the_actual_retraining_rule[1]] [6]. The OOS equity curve is therefore a sequence of decisions that could have been made at each historical refit date, not a curve produced by fitting once on the full sample.

Let event i have feature vector X_i available at its decision time t_i0 and label-realization time t_i1. In financial labeling, the label span [t_i0, t_i1] matters because it is the price path used to determine y_i [walk_forward_folds_simulate_the_actual_retraining_rule[2]] [7]. A fold should therefore specify: the train event set, any inner validation set used to choose hyperparameters, the test event set, the label spans attached to both sets, the information cutoff, execution lag, and the performance metric. Fit scalers, imputers, feature selectors, calibrators, and models only after the fold's eligible train set has been determined. If hyperparameters are selected, use an inner validation procedure inside the outer train period; the outer OOS period is not a tuning set.

A practical WFO loop is:

1. Sort events by decision time and retain each event's actual label end time.
2. Select an expanding or rolling train window ending before the OOS block.
3. Define the OOS block and remove any training event whose label span overlaps it.
4. Apply an embargo when the candidate training set contains observations after the test block or when the surrounding design requires a post-test dependence buffer.
5. Fit each candidate pipeline from scratch on the permitted train data.
6. Generate predictions at the natural event or bar cadence, convert them to positions, apply execution, costs, and sizing, and record only OOS strategy returns.
7. Append the OOS returns to the chronological ledger and refit at the next scheduled date.

The last step is the key discipline. Do not average fold accuracies and call that a strategy backtest. Preserve timestamps, positions, fills, costs, and returns so that turnover, drawdown, exposure, and risk-adjusted performance are calculated on the same stitched OOS path. WFO can use non-overlapping test blocks, but the label-aware purge still matters at the boundary: a training event that starts before the test block may have a forward label that reaches into it.

**Case study - the Bailey selection question.** Bailey et al. frame the central decision as selecting the best model configuration in-sample and then observing its relative performance out-of-sample. The first subset is used to determine the optimal configuration and the second subset tests that in-sample choice [walk_forward_folds_simulate_the_actual_retraining_rule[3]] [8]. That is a selection experiment, not merely a claim that one forecast has predictive accuracy.

The outcome is a performance path attached to a deployment rule. A WFO result can be strong because the rule is genuinely adaptive, because the selected configuration was lucky, or because the implementation leaked information. WFO addresses temporal ordering and gives a realistic path; it does not by itself estimate how often the selection process would have chosen a lucky winner.
content.purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_:
**Purging** addresses label-horizon overlap. Suppose the test labels cover a time region from a to b. Remove a training event i when its label span intersects the test region, operationally when t_i1 >= a and t_i0 <= b for closed intervals [purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_channels[0]] [7]. This catches both a pre-test training event whose forward return runs into the test period and a post-test training event whose label reaches backward into the test period. With variable triple-barrier horizons, use the actual t_i1 or exit time rather than subtracting one fixed number of rows [purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_channels[1]] [1].

**Embargo** addresses a different channel: dependence between observations immediately after the test block. After purging, remove training events whose event starts lie in (b, b + h_embargo] [purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_channels[0]] [7]. Momentum, volatility persistence, slowly changing features, and delayed information can make an observation immediately after the test period statistically dependent on it even when its label interval does not literally intersect the test interval. The Quant Lessons procedure states the same distinction: purge overlapping label horizons, then exclude a buffer after the test fold for serial-correlation leakage [purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_channels[1]] [1].

The two controls should not be collapsed into one arbitrary gap. Purging is determined by the intersection of label intervals. Embargo is determined by a dependence buffer after the test region. A source describes an embargo of ceil(delta*T) samples in one setup and notes that its size is often on the order of the label horizon, but that is a design choice, not a universal constant [purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_channels[0]] [7]. Estimate it from the dependence and feature-construction process, document it, and stress it.

The fold algorithm is consequently: partition without shuffling; identify the test interval and all test label spans; remove every train event with an intersecting label span; remove post-test train events in the embargo interval; fit preprocessing and the model on what remains; evaluate on the test set [purge_and_embargo_two_different_leakage_channels[1]] [1]. In CPCV, where training groups can exist on both sides of selected test groups, this rule is essential. In a strictly one-sided WFO fold whose train set ends before the test block, there may be no post-test training rows to embargo. That is not permission to omit embargo from a general purged-CV implementation; it means the particular WFO geometry has no eligible rows on that side.

A common bad shortcut is to drop the last h rows of the train set for every fold. It can be conservative for a fixed-horizon label, but it fails for variable horizons, irregular event times, multiple test intervals, and features with a longer dependence horizon. The correct invariant is interval intersection plus an explicitly chosen post-test buffer. Also audit feature timestamps: purging labels cannot rescue a feature that was itself computed with future information.
content.cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_select:
CPCV first partitions the ordered sample into N contiguous groups. It selects k groups as the test set in every combination, so the number of train/test splits is binom(N,k); an example with N = 6 and k = 2 produces 15 combinations [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[0]] [2]. Fit a fresh model on the eligible train events for each combination, apply purge and embargo, and score the selected test groups. The implementation pattern explicitly uses test-fold start and end indices, a test-split count, and a mapping from test indices into a backtest path [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[1]] [4].

Do not confuse the number of split fits with the number of complete paths. The AFML path construction is:

- Number of split fits: C(N,k) = binom(N,k).
- Number of complete paths: phi = (k/N) * C(N,k) = C(N-1,k-1).
- Each complete path contains one OOS result for each of the N groups in chronological order.
- Each group is tested in C(N-1,k-1) combinations, which is why those combinations can be assigned into that many full paths.

AFML CPCV has 15 test combinations/models and 5 complete backtest paths, with φ = (k/N) * C(N,k); the N=6,k=2 example is not explicitly stated. [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[2]] [11]

For N = 6 and k = 2, the design fits 15 split models and reconstructs 5 paths. The 15 split scores are not 15 independent full histories, and concatenating every split's OOS observations into one oversized equity curve double-counts dates. Reconstruct each path separately, calculate path-level returns and risk statistics, and report the distribution rather than only its most favorable member. CPCV gives broader path coverage than one WFO sequence, but it costs more computation and its selected test groups need not form one single contiguous interval across the whole sample; the base groups remain ordered and unshuffled [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[1]] [4].

CSCV in Bailey's PBO framework is related but not identical. Divide the performance history into S equal subperiods. For every symmetric partition, one half is IS and its complement is OOS; complementary assignments are treated symmetrically. The paper's count of unique combinations is:

C_S = (1/2) * binom(S, S/2).

For each c from 1 to C_S, evaluate M candidate configurations on both halves. Let R_IS(m,c) and R_OOS(m,c) be the chosen performance statistic. Select the IS winner m*_c:

m*_c = argmax_m R_IS(m,c).

Rank that same configuration among all M OOS performances, with the rank oriented so that a better performance has a higher rank. Then use the paper's relative rank and logit:

omega_c = rank_OOS(m*_c) / (M + 1)

lambda_c = ln(omega_c / (1 - omega_c)).

The empirical estimator is:

PBO_hat = (1 / C_S) * sum from c = 1 to C_S of I(lambda_c < 0).

The paper describes this as the rate at which optimal IS strategies underperform the median OOS, and gives the population definition as a probability-weighted event in which the OOS rank of the IS-optimal strategy is below the median [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[3]] [8] [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[3]] [8]. It defines the rank relative to M + 1 and the logit exactly as above [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[3]] [8].

Three formula details prevent many bad PBO implementations. First, use the unique symmetric count C_S; evaluating both a partition and its complement as separate observations is a different bookkeeping convention and must not be silently compared with the C_S denominator. Second, if a library returns rank 1 for the best OOS strategy, reverse it before using omega = rank/(M+1), because the paper's positive logit means better OOS consistency. Third, count the negative-logit cases; do not use the mean logit, the fraction of negative returns, or one WFO Sharpe as PBO. Ties, rank direction, the metric, and the candidate universe must be declared.

**Case study - Bailey et al.'s four-subperiod illustration.** The paper illustrates the construction with four subsamples A, B, C, and D grouped into two halves [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[3]] [8]. Each half is alternately used as the training or IS subset and the other half as the testing or OOS subset; running all configurations produces a relative-ranking logit for each combination [cpcv_and_cscv_many_paths_versus_a_selection_statistic[3]] [8]. The decision is therefore repeated selection under many complementary histories, not one lucky split.

The outcome is a distribution of logits. Positive values indicate that the IS choice tends to retain a strong relative OOS rank, while negative values are the PBO events. That case reveals the scope of PBO: it diagnoses the reliability of a selection procedure over a defined set of trials. It does not certify that the champion has positive net returns, that the market is stationary, or that an unrecorded research trial could not have been selected.
content.expanding_versus_rolling_walk_forward_wi:
Both windows preserve chronological order. They differ in which historical regimes the model is allowed to use at each refit.

| Window | Training set at refit j | Embedded assumption | Main benefit | Main failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expanding / anchored | All eligible events from the initial start through the current cutoff | Older and newer regimes remain useful, with more data generally helping estimation | More observations, lower parameter variance, and greater stability | Old regimes can dilute a current regime or preserve obsolete relationships |
| Rolling / sliding | A fixed recent interval ending at the current cutoff | Recent data is more relevant than distant data | Adapts faster to drift and limits stale history | Fewer observations, higher estimation variance, and dependence on the chosen window length |

The anchored definition starts at the beginning and grows, whereas the rolling definition has fixed length and slides forward [expanding_versus_rolling_walk_forward_windows[0]] [6]. Rolling therefore encodes an explicit belief that the recent past matters most [expanding_versus_rolling_walk_forward_windows[0]] [6]. Expanding is not automatically more conservative: if the data-generating process changes, old observations can be a source of bias. Rolling is not automatically more realistic: a short window can make feature scaling, class balance, and risk estimates unstable.

**Decision rule.** Choose the window using information available before the final evaluation, then stress nearby lengths and both regimes. If only one window length works, report that fragility. Do not select expanding versus rolling by looking at the same OOS path repeatedly and calling the winner an independent validation. The window policy is part of the candidate configuration and belongs in the trial universe if it was searched.

A useful contrast is mechanism rather than slogan. Expanding windows reduce sampling noise by pooling history; rolling windows reduce regime staleness by discarding history. Neither changes the need for label-aware purging, train-only preprocessing, cost-aware returns, or an untouched final holdout.
content.implementation_failure_modes_what_invali:
| Mistake | Why it is wrong | Correct implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Rank classification accuracy in PBO | Accuracy ranks a forecast-label task, not necessarily the economic strategy produced by the forecasts. Payoff asymmetry, costs, sizing, and turnover can make the accuracy winner different from the return winner. | Convert predictions to positions, simulate fills and costs, and rank the declared net strategy metric consistently in IS and OOS. |
| Split rows while ignoring label spans | A train row can start before the test row but have a forward label realized inside the test interval. | Store t_i0 and t_i1 and purge by interval intersection [implementation_failure_modes_what_invalidates_the_result[0]] [7]. |
| Skip embargo because labels do not overlap | Adjacent post-test observations can still share serial dependence through features or returns. | Remove post-test train starts for a documented dependence buffer when the fold geometry contains such rows [implementation_failure_modes_what_invalidates_the_result[0]] [7]. |
| Fit a scaler or selector globally | Statistics computed using future folds change the representation seen by the model and leak test information. | Fit every learned preprocessing object inside each fold. The fold procedure explicitly trains only after the permitted train set is formed [implementation_failure_modes_what_invalidates_the_result[1]] [1]. |
| Write a fold model to a live path | A later fold, evaluator, or production process can load the wrong state; even without a direct leak, the run can overwrite the artifact intended for live use. | Use in-memory state or run/fold/trial-specific immutable artifact locations. Promote one final artifact only after all validation and holdout decisions are complete. |
| Stride or subsample OOS bars | Skipping bars omits signals, fills, holding-period transitions, and costs. The resulting PnL is not the declared strategy's OOS distribution. | Evaluate every event/bar needed by execution. If the strategy truly trades every q bars, define that event universe before labels and folds are created. |
| Reuse OOS to choose features, windows, or thresholds | The OOS period becomes another training signal, so the reported OOS performance is no longer untouched. | Freeze the trial universe and decisions before the final OOS run; use nested validation or a separate holdout for later choices. |
| Treat all CPCV split scores as independent paths | The same dates occur in multiple split combinations. | Reconstruct complete paths and report path-level distributions; do not concatenate duplicate OOS dates. |

Bailey et al. emphasize that the ranking procedure is generic in the performance measure rather than tied to one prediction metric. The ranking procedure is generic across performance metrics, including Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Jensen's Alpha, and Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio. [implementation_failure_modes_what_invalidates_the_result[2]] [8] For a trading strategy, that means the candidate object being compared should include the full pipeline: features, model, threshold, position mapping, sizing, rebalance rule, and cost assumptions. If the production objective is net Sharpe, use the same declared net-return construction for selection and OOS ranking; do not select on accuracy and then advertise PBO for Sharpe.

**Case study - MLFinLab's path bookkeeping.** The MLFinLab CPCV source makes a useful structural decision: it retains test-fold start and end indices, tracks the number of test splits, and maps test indices into a backtest path [implementation_failure_modes_what_invalidates_the_result[3]] [4]. The outcome of that design is path identity: a researcher can calculate a complete chronological OOS history instead of treating every test combination as a separate full history.

That bookkeeping does not, by itself, solve metric leakage, live-artifact contamination, feature look-ahead, or skipped-bar evaluation. The library-level split object should be surrounded by a run harness that resets model state, isolates artifacts, records the exact trial universe, and stores one row per OOS event with prediction, position, fill, cost, and return. Validation is a data-and-software boundary, not only an index generator.
content.a_reproducible_validation_protocol:
Use the following protocol when the objective is an ML trading strategy rather than a standalone classifier.

1. **Freeze the information set.** For every feature, record its publication or availability timestamp, lookback, and computation delay. For every label, record t_i0 and actual t_i1. Include execution latency and the cost model.
2. **Define the candidate universe.** Enumerate all model families, feature sets, hyperparameters, thresholds, window choices, and position rules that may be selected. PBO is conditional on this universe; silently excluding failed experiments makes the selection problem look smaller than it was.
3. **Choose the outer geometry.** Use WFO when the primary question is performance under a known live retraining schedule. Add purging at label boundaries. Use CPCV when path dependence and a distribution of OOS paths matter; choose N and k before inspecting the final results.
4. **Generate labels and folds without future access.** Keep the actual event intervals. For every test combination, purge all intersecting train labels and embargo eligible post-test train events. Do not replace this with a row-count gap unless the label and event geometry genuinely justify it.
5. **Train in isolation.** For each fold and trial, fit preprocessing, model, calibration, and selection state from scratch. Save artifacts only in fold-specific locations, or keep them in memory. A production model is not a fold cache.
6. **Score the strategy at full cadence.** Produce predictions, positions, fills, costs, and net returns for every OOS event or bar. Store a fold identifier, path identifier, and timestamp so duplicated CPCV test observations can be reconstructed rather than accidentally pooled.
7. **Calculate the right diagnostics.** Report path-level net return, Sharpe or other declared metric, drawdown, turnover, exposure, hit rate, and the distribution across CPCV paths. Hit rate is descriptive; it is not a replacement for the economic selection metric.
8. **Calculate PBO separately.** Apply CSCV to the M candidate performance series using the unique symmetric count C_S. For each partition, select the IS winner, rank that winner among all M OOS candidates, compute omega and lambda, and count lambda < 0. Keep PBO separate from the WFO equity curve.
9. **Run a final holdout.** After window, feature, model, cost, and trial-universe choices are frozen, evaluate once on a later period not used for those choices. A low PBO does not make a final holdout optional.

This protocol creates an auditable ledger. Every reported number can be traced to a timestamp, an allowed information set, a fold, a candidate configuration, an execution rule, and a path. It also makes a negative result useful: if all paths fail after costs, the model is not rescued by a high classification score; if only one window or path succeeds, the fragility is visible.
content.synthesis_three_tools_three_questions:
| Tool | Primary question | Fold geometry | Output | Main trade-off | What it cannot prove |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Walk-forward | Would this fixed retraining policy have worked in chronological deployment? | One sequence of past-train, future-test blocks; expanding or rolling | One stitched OOS path | Strong temporal realism, limited path diversity | That the selected configuration was not lucky among many trials |
| CPCV | How does the strategy behave across many purged train/test arrangements and reconstructed histories? | N ordered groups, k test groups, C(N,k) split fits, phi full paths | Distribution of path-level OOS results | More path coverage, more computation and overlapping reuse of dates | That the candidate universe or feature set was chosen without research bias |
| PBO / CSCV | How often does the IS selection rule choose a configuration that falls below the OOS median? | S subperiods, C_S = (1/2) * binom(S,S/2) symmetric IS/OOS partitions, M trials | Distribution of OOS rank logits and PBO_hat | Explicit selection-risk diagnosis, relative and trial-set dependent | Profitability, absence of leakage, or probability of a live loss |

The central tension is between realism, coverage, and selection awareness. WFO is closest to the live clock but can be dominated by one particular sequence of regimes. CPCV changes the question from one historical route to many combinatorial routes, but it reuses observations across splits and therefore requires path reconstruction and careful dependence controls. PBO goes one level higher: it evaluates the selection mechanism itself, not only the final selected path.

A second tension is that more validation can create more opportunities to overfit validation. Choosing rolling rather than expanding, changing the embargo, selecting k, dropping a feature, and changing the PBO metric are all research decisions. If they were informed by OOS results, they belong in the selection history. The cure is not to avoid diagnostics; it is to freeze decision stages, record the candidate universe, and reserve a final holdout.

The recommended division of labor is therefore: use WFO to test the operational updating rule; use purged and embargoed CPCV to obtain path distributions; use Bailey-style CSCV/PBO to quantify relative selection failure; and use a final holdout to challenge the frozen design. Interpret a low PBO as evidence that the IS winner is usually not below the OOS median within the tested universe, not as a guarantee of positive returns. A strategy that passes all four layers is more credible; none of the layers can repair a feature timestamp, label, execution, or artifact bug.
